doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Transcribing as bread and butter and ear training
summary: Bailey recalls a box of transcriptions of Clifford Brown, Dexter Gordon and Wes, and explains how transcribing trains the ear, starting with bass and melody.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: And another thing that you had mentioned I read, you said transcribing was your bread and butter as far as understanding harmony and improvisation. So you did a lot of that?

Yeah. I did a ton of that, and I wish I had time to do more. But you know I actually didn’t even realize ‘til actually when I was moving my stuff from my New York apartment to the Boston apartment and I just had files that I hadn’t opened for years. And I came across this box of transcription I had done that I had stuff from high school and through my time at Berklee and after. And there were stacks, and there was a ton of Clifford Brown, Dexter Gordon, and Wes — and there was just so — I had forgotten that I’d done all that work. I was like wow, you did do your homework. I think it’s essential at some point in your development. And we could say that if you’re a rock player or whatever style you play, at some point to dig in to that language, whatever language that you’re fascinated in and learn as much as you can from it.
Do you recall when you did all that transcribing if you then — well first of all did you transcribe the chord changes first?

Mmm. That’s a great question. I think over time I developed it. At first I think I would find some chart for it. But this was also great, what’s great about transcribing is it’s the best ear training. So my advice to folks, or if I’m going to do it now, if I’m going to write a chart I usually get the bass first, the melody, and then again it’s sort of like the sandwich. What’s the flavor of the sandwich. Is it a minor sandwich? Is it a major sandwich? Or is it major sandwich with a — there’s something else in there. Oh that’s sharp 5 or it’s a major sandwich with a flat 5. You know what I mean? But eventually it gets your ear to be able to hear the whole sandwich in time, where you can just sort of do that. So it’s a process you know. But I think it’s the best way to really learn how to hear harmony.
